newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan coal mine closes, signalling end of era.
newsitem.headline: Japan coal mine closes, signalling end of era.

text.p: Japan's largest and oldest coal mine was shut down on Sunday, a sign of the likely demise of a once-powerful industry that helped fuel Japan's massive industrial base.
Helmeted miners finishing their last shifts fought back tears in the closing ceremony of the Miike mine in southern Fukuoka Prefecture, operated by Mitsui Coal Mining Co Ltd for 124 years.

In a message to assembled miners, company executives and union leaders, International Trade and Industry Minister Shinji Sato acknowledged the role the mine had played in Japan's industrial development.
"We are solemnly facing the closure of the Miike mine, which has played a major role in the nation's modernisation and industrialisation," his message said.

Nearly 2,000 people will be laid off by Miike's demise, which leaves two remaining coal mines -- in northern Hokkaido and southern Nagasaki -- facing a grim future after government subsidies for domestic coal, which is priced three times higher than imports, dry up in 2002.
However, Japan's nine big electric utilities say they are moving to boost coal use to an estimated 15 percent of the energy supply by 2006, up from 10 percent in 1996.

Fuelling the switch to coal is government eagerness to reduce dependence on oil imports and a deep distrust of nuclear power among the public in Japan, which has been aggravated recently by the worst nuclear power accident in Japan's history.

A March 11 fire and explosion at the Tokaimura nuclear waste reprocessing plant, 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo, exposed 37 workers to radiation and left the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC) which manages the plant reeling from harsh criticism following revelations of a bungled emergency operation and lack of preparedness.
The public relations disaster of Tokaimura exacerbated fears after an attempt to cover up an accident last year at the Monju prototype fast-breeder reactor run by PNC in western Japan.
Japan plans to reach 50 percent energy self-sufficiency by the early 21st century using plutonium technology.
